items.title: An Anti-Adhesive Hydrogel Delivering Ginger-Derived Exosome-Like Nanoparticles Reshapes the Neuroinflammatory Microenvironment After Traumatic Brain Injury.
items.authors: Jie Chen; Tong Zhu; Jinpeng Wen; Mengqing Shen; Beilin Hou; Boyuan Gu; Mingxia Zhang; Siyu Sun
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers secondary injury involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting the need for multi-target therapies. Ginger-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (GELNs) offer multi-target therapeutic potential but are limited by insufficient local retention and rapid clearance. TBI-induced brain-skull adhesion may further aggravate the pathological environment. To address these limitations, an anti-adhesive hydrogel (CG) composed of methacrylated chondroitin sulfate and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine is loaded with GELNs to form CG-GELNs. CG-GELNs attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion and provides greater behavioral benefits than free GELNs, including reduced anxiety-like behavior, improved social novelty discrimination, and enhanced spatial memory. At the pathological level, CG-GELNs confers coordinated protection against secondary injury by preserving blood-brain barrier integrity, suppressing pro-inflammatory responses, mitigating mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, and ultimately preserving synaptic function. Mechanistically, GELNs-associated microRNA-396 (miR-396) suppresses secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) expression, and functional rescue experiments support the contribution of this miR-396/SPP1 axis to the anti-inflammatory effects of GELNs in microglial cells. Overall, CG-GELNs simultaneously improves localized delivery of GELNs, attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion, and suppresses neuroinflammation, offering a potentially translatable therapeutic platform for remodeling the neuroinflammatory microenvironment and promoting neurological recovery after TBI.

items.title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Lluís Camprubí-Ferrer; Jesús Soldán-Hidalgo; Emil Axell; Marzia Dell'Eva; Marta García-Cruzado; Juan García-Revilla; Yiyi Yang; Rosalía Fernández-Calle
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3+ microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1+ dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

items.title: Intranasal delivery of a ROS-activatable myeloperoxidase inhibitor alleviates Alzheimer's-like symptoms and pathology.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Jing Wang; Peilin Cong; Enduo Feng; Matthias W G Zeller; Boyu Zhang; Yifan Lv; Negin Jalali Motlagh; Jenny Linnoila
items.abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are important contributors to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a key driver of oxidative inflammation released mainly by activated microglia in the neurodegenerative brain, is a potential therapeutic target to inhibit the neuroinflammatory cascade and oxidative damage in AD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, and achieving targeted brain delivery of an MPO inhibitor and minimizing systemic effects remain significant challenges. We addressed these limitations by first establishing that genetic deletion of MPO in the 5XFAD mouse model improved memory performance and reduced amyloid deposition, validating MPO as a therapeutic target. We then developed a liposome-encapsulated reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable MPO inhibitor (LERAMI). LERAMI uniquely combines targeted delivery with on-demand drug release, utilizing a ROS-sensitive linker to selectively release MPO inhibitors in ROS-rich regions within the AD microenvironment, minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In the 5XFAD mouse model. By reducing MPO expression and activity, LERAMI significantly improved cognitive performance, accompanied by decreased microglial activation, attenuated oxidative DNA damage, improved synaptic and neuronal density, and reduced amyloid burden. RNA sequencing revealed a robust hippocampal transcriptomic reprogramming, with upregulation of pathways critical for synaptic plasticity, calcium signaling, axon guidance, and neuroprotection, along with downregulation of inflammatory and immune response pathways. These findings demonstrate that targeted ROS-activatable MPO inhibition with LERAMI represents a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and potentially other neuroinflammatory diseases, offering a unique approach to mitigate neuroinflammation, preserve synaptic integrity, and restore cognitive function.

items.title: Human nasal turbinate derived neural crest stem cells attenuate neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration by suppressing the HMGB1-RAGE-NF-κB axis in Parkinson's disease.
items.authors: Junwon Choi; Jeong Hyeon Lee; Jung Ho Jeon; Sun Hwa Park; Hyun Ji Lee; Seung Yeon Yoo; Min Young Ahn; Dong-In Kim
items.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and persistent neuroinflammation. Although stem cell-based therapies have shown therapeutic potential, effective control of the inflammatory niche in the diseased brain is critical for improving their therapeutic efficacy. This study investigated whether human nasal turbinate derived neural crest stem cells (hNTSCs) protect dopaminergic neurons by regulating microglia-mediated inflammation through the high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1)-Receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE)-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling pathway. In vitro, hNTSC co-culture reduced 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+)-induced microglial activation and HMGB1 expression in Human microglial clone 3 (HMC3) cells. Conditioned medium from MPP+-stimulated microglia increased RAGE expression and NF-κB phosphorylation in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived dopaminergic neurons, whereas conditioned medium from hNTSC-co-cultured microglia attenuated these changes. In 9-month-old male mice with 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced parkinsonism, hNTSC transplantation reduced microglial activation and HMGB1 expression in the substantia nigra. Treatment also decreased RAGE expression and the p-NF-κB/NF-κB ratio, preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor performance in open-field and rotarod tests. These findings indicate that hNTSCs reduce microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neuronal damage, at least in part, by suppressing the HMGB1-RAGE-NF-κB signaling pathway. hNTSCs may provide a cell-based therapeutic approach for modulating the inflammatory lesion environment in PD.

items.title: Inhibition of NLRP3 maintains microglial architecture and enhances neurological recovery after traumatic brain injury.
items.authors: Sergio Castro-Gomez; Luis José Medina-Centanaro; Juan Ignacio Muñoz-Manco; Ana Vieira-Saecker; Sharumathi Jeyasankar; Ida Kulińska; Tao Li; Felix D Weiss
items.abstract: The NLR family pyrin domain containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome orchestrates neuroinflammation, but its role in traumatic brain injury (TBI) and the therapeutic value of pharmacological inhibition remain incompletely defined. Using Nlrp3-deficient mice and two novel orally bioavailable selective antagonists (NP3-253 and NP3-361), we investigate NLRP3-dependent mechanisms of post-traumatic neuroinflammation and functional recovery. After controlled cortical impact, NLRP3 inflammasome components, pro-inflammatory genes, and mediators are robustly upregulated during the first post-injury week. Genetic Nlrp3 deletion and post-TBI NP3-253 treatment preserve microglial architecture and reduce aggregation and redistribution of the inflammasome adaptor apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC), while post-TBI NP3-253 and NP3-361 therapeutically accelerate neurological recovery during treatment. Longitudinal intravital imaging shows that pre-TBI NLRP3 inhibition with NP3-361 constrains post-traumatic microglial activation in vivo. These findings establish NLRP3 as a driver of post-traumatic microglial morphodynamics and support selective NLRP3 inhibition as a promising strategy to improve neurological outcomes after TBI.

items.title: Neuronal IL-34 programs microglial activity via the TGF-β-MEF2C axis to constrain neuroinflammation following brain ischemia.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Minshu Li; Xu Zhou; Ran Li; Hanchen Liu; Caiyun Qi; Wenjun Zhang; Yali Han; Tingyu Yin
items.abstract: Brain ischemia induces robust neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation, yet whether ischemic neurons actively reprogram microglial phenotypes to limit inflammation remains elusive. Here, we identify neuronal interleukin-34 (IL-34) as a critical immunomodulatory signal that maintains microglial homeostasis after cerebral ischemia. We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of Il34 (Syn1-Il34tg mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal Il34 knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures (P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1), while suppressing inflammatory activities (Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific Mef2c overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β-MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

items.title: Maternal gluten diet exacerbates offspring autistic-like behaviors through the gut-brain axis mediated by gut microbial metabolite elaidic acid.
items.authors: Senbao Xu; Zaoxuan Wu; Daixuan Zhou; Yunying Gong; Ye Ouyang; Xiuying Liu; Shuze Chen; Jun Huang
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental conditions characterized by social deficits and stereotyped behaviors, for which effective treatments remain lacking. Here we investigated whether early-life gluten exposure exacerbates autism-like behaviors in BTBR mice and explored the underlying microbiota-metabolite-brain mechanism. Early-life gluten exposure aggravated social avoidance, anxiety, and repetitive behaviors in BTBR offspring, accompanied by reduced mushroom dendritic spine density and diminished microglial branch complexity in the hippocampus. Microbiota sequencing revealed gut microbial dysbiosis, with increased abundance of Hungatella hathewayi and Eubacterium sp. Marseille-P4003. Consistent with their capacity for lipid transformation, untargeted metabolomics showed enrichment of unsaturated fatty acid metabolism and elevated fecal elaidic acid levels. Clinically, targeted quantification confirmed that fecal elaidic acid was significantly higher in children with ASD than in their healthy siblings. Supporting a causal role, exogenous elaidic acid administration dose-dependently worsened behavioral deficits and induced hippocampal spine loss and amoeboid microglial activation. Mechanistically, intestinal transcriptomics revealed activation of antigen processing and presentation and cytokine signaling pathways, whereas hippocampal transcriptomics showed downregulation of immune negative regulators (Egr2, Egr4) alongside enrichment of MHC-I and TNF pathways, indicating impaired central immune restraint. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that early-life gluten exposure induces gut microbiota dysbiosis that drives elaidic acid accumulation, which in turn activates intestinal immunity and suppresses hippocampal immune negative regulation via the gut-brain axis, ultimately aggravating neuroinflammation and autism-like behaviors.

items.title: High-throughput screening of patient iPSC-derived neurons identifies the gut microbial metabolites that attenuate Alzheimer's disease pathology.
items.authors: Dhruv Gohel; Amit Kumar Gupta; Yichen Li; Zhibing Tan; Amy C Burrows; Anthony J Horak; Yuan Hou; Zhigang Liu
items.abstract: Gut microbiota-derived metabolites influence the gut-brain axis and may impact Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. However, the microbial metabolites involved in this process and their functional roles are largely unknown. We screened 352 gut metabolites in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived neurons from individuals with AD to identify compounds that reduce tau hyperphosphorylation. We identified agmatine as a lead candidate, which decreased hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons and cerebral organoids. In 5xFAD mice, agmatine (100 mg/kg/day) improved cognition, reduced amyloid plaques, lowered neuroinflammation, and increased beneficial gut bacteria, including Agathobacter and Bacteroides. Transcriptomic analysis showed that agmatine downregulated complement and inflammatory genes (C1QB, C2, C3AR1, CCL3, CXCL8, and CXCL6) in patient iPSC-derived cerebral organoids. Agmatine also decreased C3aR and pSTAT3 levels in vivo, mechanistically supporting the reduced tau phosphorylation in iPSC-derived neurons. Altogether, these findings identified the therapeutic potential of gut-derived metabolites and identified agmatine as potential treatment for AD.

items.title: Biophysical and Physiological Preconditioning of Mesenchymal Stem Cells: From Environmental Sensing to Extracellular Vesicle Production.
items.authors: Mohd Fahmi ElMotasem; Hiroyo Kondo; Noriaki Maeshige; Hidemi Fujino
items.abstract: Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) have been shown to possess the paracrine regenerative effects of MSCs, making them attractive therapeutic options that avoid challenges associated with direct MSC transplantation. To control and improve EV function, preconditioning of MSCs prior to EV isolation has been performed using a multitude of methods including hypoxia, mechanical stress, and metabolic disruption. While preconditioning has been reported to enhance EV yield and alter EV-associated miRNA profiles, the exact intracellular signaling pathways connecting the stimulus to the final EV phenotype remain fragmented across the literature. In this review, we aim to compile the existing knowledge and synthesize a proposed framework where the process from MSC sensing of external stress to EV release and miRNA loading can be visualized and better understood. Preconditioning stimuli are sensed by MSCs through different sensing mechanisms but converge on central signaling hubs such as HIF-1α, PI3K/Akt, ERK, calcium/Rho, and mTOR. These hubs then connect to EV biogenesis and release proteins such as nSMase2, ESCRT-associated proteins, Rab GTPases, and RNA-binding proteins. EV-associated miRNA profiles also showed recurring changes under particular preconditioning conditions, such as miR-210 showing consistent enrichment under hypoxia. The proposed framework can help researchers better understand and develop targeted methods of preconditioning in MSCs.

items.title: Inflammation-Licensed MSCs Attenuate Acute Spinal Cord Injury by Suppressing NET Formation and Limiting Neutrophil Recruitment.
items.authors: Yifan Liu; Haoyue Hu; Shulong Yin; Linquan Li; Han Zheng; Yi Chen; Wenxiang Li; Sheng Liu
items.abstract: Acute spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a rapidly evolving secondary injury cascade shaped by a hostile inflammatory microenvironment. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have shown therapeutic potential in SCI, but acute-phase transplantation remains challenging because this milieu compromises MSC survival and therapeutic efficacy. Here, we developed a disease-context inflammatory licensing strategy using tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) to generate inflammation-licensed hUCMSCs, termed TIIMSCs, with enhanced immunomodulatory properties and prolonged in vivo persistence. In the SCI mouse model, TIIMSCs reduced acute inflammatory cytokine expression, limited neutrophil recruitment, and suppressed neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, accompanied by improved functional recovery and histological repair. Mechanistically, inflammatory licensing upregulated cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2) in TIIMSCs, leading to increased prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production, which acted on neutrophils through prostaglandin E receptor 4 (EP4) to activate protein kinase A (PKA) and inhibit extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation, thereby suppressing NET formation. In parallel, TIIMSCs shifted microglia toward a more reparative phenotype and attenuated a microglia-associated chemotactic program, thereby reducing neutrophil recruitment. Together, these findings identify disease-context inflammatory licensing as a rational strategy to adapt MSCs to the acute SCI microenvironment and provide a potential framework for overcoming clinical barriers to effective acute-phase cell transplantation.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Cortical and meningeal neuroimmune interactions contribute to the generation of migraine headaches.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Şefik Evren Erdener; Zeynep Kaya; Turgay Dalkara
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Migraine is a prevalent disorder that ranks as the second leading cause of disability among all diseases. Recent advancements have significantly enhanced our comprehension of its underlying pathophysiology. Growing evidence highlights complex neuroimmune signaling networks-particularly interactions between meningeal nociceptors and resident immune cells-as key contributors to headache generation. The clinical success of anti-calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antibodies underscores the importance of intercellular communication between the dural nociceptive nerves and adjacent resident immune cells such as macrophages in migraine headache. Notably, the intercellular inflammatory interplay is not confined to the meninges. Disturbances within the brain parenchyma potentially act as initiating triggers, as suggested by the presence of aura and premonitory symptoms preceding the headache. Recent experimental discoveries indicate that neuronal stress triggers an inflammatory signaling cascade that, through interactions with astrocytes and microglia, propagates to the meninges, ultimately inducing meningeal neurogenic inflammation and headache. This model is supported by converging experimental evidence and human imaging studies employing PET and quantitative MRI, which document the presence of changes compatible with inflammatory activity within the brain parenchyma and overlying meninges of patients with migraine with aura. Genetic studies identifying several inflammation-related genes and pathways as risk factors for migraine further corroborate this concept. Furthermore, cell-specific transcriptomic analyses of mouse brains have revealed astrocyte-selective activation of nuclear factor kappa B -regulated inflammatory transcriptional pathways after cortical spreading depolarization, the neurophysiological correlate of migraine aura. Owing to their extensive interface with the cerebrospinal fluid, astrocytes are uniquely positioned to release inflammatory mediators to activate meningeal nociceptors and immune cells. Insights from pain research suggest that neuroimmune interactions may be responsible for the widespread parenchymal increases in 18 kDa translocator protein (TSPO) PET signals observed in migraine with aura patients. This discovery also identifies TSPO as a potential player in migraine pathophysiology and novel drug target. In this review, by integrating cellular and molecular findings from peripheral pain and inflammation research, we examine the dynamic interactions between neurons and glia, as well as between meningeal nociceptors and immune cells in the context of migraine headache. This perspective provides a conceptual framework for understanding how nociceptors and glial cells coordinate to signal non-homeostatic brain states-initiating protective, tightly regulated responses without progressing to overt neuroinflammatory disease and provides novel insight into the findings of PET studies involving TSPO.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Weimin Zhang; Yu Zhao; Priya Prakash; Heather Appleby; Kelly Barriball; Simona Capponi; Qingwen Jiang; Aleksandra M Wudzinska
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Human retrotransposon insertions are often associated with diseases. Regarding neurodegenerative X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a human-specific SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) subfamily F retrotransposon was inserted in intron 32 of the TAF1 gene. Here, we genomically rewrote a portion of the mouse Taf1 allele with the corresponding 78-kb XDP patient-derived TAF1 allele. In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), the presence of the intronic SVA-rather than the hybrid gene structure-reduces hyTAF1 (hybrid TAF1 mRNA) levels. This leads to transcriptional downregulation of genes with TATA boxes enriched in their promoters and triggers apoptosis. Chromatin and transcriptome profiling revealed that intronic SVAs are actively transcribed, forming barriers that likely impede transcription elongation. In mice, neuronal-lineage TAF1 humanization resulted in lethality in male progeny within 2 months. XDP male mice developed severe atrophy centered on the striatum-the same brain region affected in XDP patients. Lastly, CRISPRa-mediated activation of hyTAF1 restored mESC viability, suggesting that boosting TAF1 transcription could be a therapeutic approach.

top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Zhechun Hu; Yujian Luo; Tingqi Zhou; Xuan Wu; Jiao Ma; Chao Wang; Liang Wang; Xiao-Dong Wang
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Identification of Type 1 and Type 2 α-Synuclein-Seeds by CSF Seed Amplification Assay in Patients With Movement Disorders.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Sandrina K Weber; Carly M Farris; Yihua Ma; Susana Schnell; Maritta Starke; Jens Ebentheuer; Jesusa E Kalinkara-Gomez; Michael Bartl
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: A novel α-synuclein (syn) seed amplification assay (synSAA) differentiates 2 types of syn-seeds in CSF: type1, associated with Lewy bodies (LBs), and type2, associated with glial-cytoplasmic inclusions, the hallmark of multiple system atrophy (MSA). However, syn-copathology extends beyond synucleinopathies, and copathologies are increasingly relevant. Different syn-seeds have been assessed in highly characterized research cohorts, but data assessing type and frequency in patients from routine clinical encounters are lacking. Hence, our objective was to determine frequency, type, and clinical association of different syn-seeds in CSF in a large cohort from a movement disorders (MDs) clinic. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included consecutive patients from a MD clinic between 2009 and 2025. CSF was tested with synSAA and clinical data derived from medical records. RESULTS: We recruited 1,059 patients (mean age 70.5 ± 10.5 years; 38.4% female; mean disease duration 4.0 ± 4.6 years). Syn-seeds were detected in 54.2% of patients, with type1-seeds predominating (88.5%). High synSAA positivity was observed in Parkinson disease (PD) (84.7%), dementia with LB (93.4%), MSA (84.5%), isolated REM-sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) (80.0%), and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) with PD (87.0%). Undetermined hypokinetic MD showed 53.7% positivity. Moderate proportions (∼25-33%) were detected in Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal syndrome, and idiopathic NPH without PD, while other neurologic disorders showed 20.9% positivity. Type2-seeds were the major seed type in MSA (79.6% of syn-seeds) and minor type in PD (6.2%), PSP (9.1%), and undetermined hypokinetic MD (13.8%). Overall, type2-seeds were present in only 2.6% of non-MSA patients. Patients with type1-seeds had worse olfaction and more hallucinations. Multivariable regression identified impaired olfaction (OR = 0.67 per point increase of identified smells out of 12, higher scores indicating better olfaction) significantly associated with type1-seeds. DISCUSSION: Our results provide reference data on syn-seed frequency in routine clinical patients, demonstrating that type1-seeds indicate common underlying syn-pathology or copathology associated with hyposmia and hallucinations. Type2-seeds are specific to MSA and detection of type2-seeds outside the clinical MSA spectrum can improve diagnosis of patients with atypical presentations because our results match neuropathologic MSA studies. In vivo identification of different seed types will improve diagnosis, clinical trial stratification, and development of targeted therapies.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Temporal interference stimulation targeting the ventromedial prefrontal cortex enhances reward learning and improves depression scores.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Feixue Wang; Mingyan Jiang; Yilan Tang; Jie Chen; Liwen Jiang; Huijuan Zhang; Long Li; Ang Li
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Reward learning depends on dynamic interactions within frontostriatal circuits that encode reward prediction errors (RPEs). Disruptions in these interactions contribute to neuropsychiatric disorders, yet noninvasive modulation of deep reward circuits remains challenging. Here, we identify frontostriatal neural dynamics underlying reward learning and develop a circuit-targeted neuromodulation approach based on transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS). Neuroimaging and computational modeling in healthy adults revealed a bidirectional excitatory-inhibitory loop between the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and ventral striatum (VS), encoding RPEs and scaling with individual learning rates. Oscillatory signatures suggested that vmPFC alpha and theta frequencies tracked RPEs, with no corresponding pattern identified for punishment processing. Alpha-frequency tTIS (10 hertz) over the vmPFC enhanced reward learning and reshaped frontostriatal connectivity, whereas theta-frequency tTIS (5 hertz) showed no effect. In a randomized trial in a cohort of 69 individuals with subclinical depression, three daily sessions of alpha-frequency tTIS alleviated subclinical depressive symptoms, with delayed benefits at 7-day follow-up. These findings provide a potential noninvasive circuit-targeted intervention for reward dysfunction and related disorders.

Disruptions in these interactions contribute to neuropsychiatric disorders, yet noninvasive modulation of deep reward circuits remains challenging. Here, we identify frontostriatal neural dynamics underlying reward learning and develop a circuit-targeted neuromodulation approach based on transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS). Neuroimaging and computational modeling in healthy adults revealed a bidirectional excitatory-inhibitory loop between the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and ventral striatum (VS), encoding RPEs and scaling with individual learning rates. Oscillatory signatures suggested that vmPFC alpha and theta frequencies tracked RPEs, with no corresponding pattern identified for punishment processing. Alpha-frequency tTIS (10 hertz) over the vmPFC enhanced reward learning and reshaped frontostriatal connectivity, whereas theta-frequency tTIS (5 hertz) showed no effect. In a randomized trial in a cohort of 69 individuals with subclinical depression, three daily sessions of alpha-frequency tTIS alleviated subclinical depressive symptoms, with delayed benefits at 7-day follow-up. These findings provide a potential noninvasive circuit-targeted intervention for reward dysfunction and related disorders.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Digital Delivery of Apolipoprotein E Genotype and Phosphorylated Tau 217 Results: The eSMARTER Randomized Clinical Trial.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Jessica B Langbaum; Claire M Erickson; Carolyn M Langlois; Elisabeth M Wood; Brian L Egleston; Kristin Harkins; Rajia Mim; Samantha John
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Patients are increasingly learning Alzheimer disease (AD) genetic and biomarker results through electronic health portals. Evaluation of alternative scalable delivery models for return of AD risk information is needed to best support patient knowledge and psychological well-being. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether a digital platform is comparable to clinician-mediated telehealth sessions for returning apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype and plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) results on outcomes of knowledge and psychological well-being. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: The Evaluation of Self-Mediated Alternatives for Risk Testing Education and Return of Results (eSMARTER) study was a noninferiority trial of a digital platform compared to clinician-mediated return of APOE genotype and optional p-tau217 results. Enrollment was conducted October 2024 through February 2025. Follow-up was completed November 2025. This was a decentralized, fully remote trial taking place across the contiguous US. Eligible participants were aged 60 to 80 years and had previously undergone APOE genotyping (without disclosure) via GeneMatch, passed psychological screening, had internet access, and could speak English. Of the 13 033 people invited by GeneMatch, 2052 accepted, and 813 were assessed for eligibility. Of 666 randomized, 651 were ultimately included. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized, 2:1, to the eSMARTER digital platform or study clinician-mediated return of APOE genotype. Following the 6-month post-APOE assessment, participants were offered optional p-tau217 disclosure via the same randomized modality. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcomes at 1 to 7 days following APOE disclosure included changes in anxiety, disease-specific distress, and AD-related knowledge within a priori noninferiority margins. RESULTS: A total of 674 persons were eligible and provided demographic information. Of these, 651 participants had been randomized to study clinician-mediated (n = 216) or digital disclosure (n = 435) and completed APOE disclosure (mean [SD] age, 68 [4.7] years; 439 [67%] female; mean [SD] telephone Montreal Cognitive Assessment score, 19 [2]; 66 [10%] APOE4 homozygotes, 377 [58%] heterozygotes, and 208 [32%] noncarriers) A total of 604 participants completed the study; 500 completed optional p-tau217 disclosure. Baseline characteristics were balanced across groups. At 1 to 7 days following APOE disclosure, scores on AD-related knowledge, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Anxiety T-score, and disease-specific distress measures met noninferiority. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Return of APOE genotype by the eSMARTER digital platform is noninferior to study clinician-mediated telehealth disclosure. No significant between-group differences were found following return of p-tau217 results. Together, these results suggest that this digital platform may provide an evidence-based scalable approach for returning AD genetic and biomarker results. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06459583.

global_hot_topics.title: Changes in Motivation and Resilience in the First Year of Medical School: A Two-Cohort Study.
global_hot_topics.authors: Phuong B Huynh; Rachel Bruyere; Heather E Harrell
global_hot_topics.abstract: Motivation and resilience are central to how medical students adapt to the demands of training, yet little is known about how these experiences change during the first year or how they may differ across cohorts exposed to different curricular environments. This study examined two consecutive first-year medical student cohorts using longitudinal measures of motivation and resilience together with open-ended student responses. Students completed the Academic Motivation Scale and Brief Resilience Scale at orientation and at the end of Year 1. Although baseline resilience did not differ significantly between cohorts, their trajectories diverged over the year (Time × Cohort: F(1,144) = 12.34, p<.001, ηp²=0.079). Resilience declined in the Class of 2027 (3.65 to 3.46, p=.003) but remained stable in the Class of 2028 (3.79 to 3.86, p=.122). Intrinsic motivation remained relatively stable in both cohorts, while extrinsic motivation increased. Open-ended responses showed that students in both cohorts experienced workload, fatigue, performance pressure, and periods of reduced motivation. The more notable difference was how students described adapting to these challenges: the later cohort more often described recovery after stress, renewed motivation following rest, and support from peers and the learning environment. Taken together, these findings suggest that resilience during the first year of medical school may be shaped not simply by the presence of stress, but by how students are supported in recovering from and adapting to it.

global_hot_topics.title: Strategic Use of Peer-to-Peer for Organised Remediation Tutoring (SUPPORT). A Retrospective Analysis.
global_hot_topics.authors: Lucas G W Bloo; J Wouters
global_hot_topics.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate examination outcomes and student experiences associated with a peer-to-peer remediation programme for undergraduate medical students with substantial academic delay. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study with an embedded qualitative survey evaluation was conducted. Medical students with at least one but less than two years of study delay were invited to join a voluntary peer-to-peer remediation programme. Examination pass rates after one academic quarter were compared between participants and non-participants using Pearson's chi-square test. Relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Participants of the programme were invited to complete an evaluation survey containing free-text questions, which were analysed qualitatively. RESULTS: A total of 69 eligible students were included in the study, all of whom were offered participation in the programme; 39 chose to join the programme (participants) and 30 did not (non-participants). Examination outcomes were available for all students. Participants had a higher pass rate than non-participants (20/39 [51.3%] vs. 8/30 [26.7%]; RR = 1.92, 95% CI 1.03-3.85; p = 0.040). A total of 23 participants completed the survey. The analysis revealed four key themes: perceived effectiveness and educational value; recognition, support, and psychological safety; need for broader and earlier implementation and organisation and logistics. CONCLUSION: Participation in the remediation programme was associated with a higher examination pass rate and positive educational, motivational, social, and emotional experiences. Earlier identification of struggling students and broader access to structured peer support may strengthen such programmes. Larger prospective studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings.

global_hot_topics.title: Identification of Type 1 and Type 2 α-Synuclein-Seeds by CSF Seed Amplification Assay in Patients With Movement Disorders.
global_hot_topics.authors: Sandrina K Weber; Carly M Farris; Yihua Ma; Susana Schnell; Maritta Starke; Jens Ebentheuer; Jesusa E Kalinkara-Gomez; Michael Bartl
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: A novel α-synuclein (syn) seed amplification assay (synSAA) differentiates 2 types of syn-seeds in CSF: type1, associated with Lewy bodies (LBs), and type2, associated with glial-cytoplasmic inclusions, the hallmark of multiple system atrophy (MSA). However, syn-copathology extends beyond synucleinopathies, and copathologies are increasingly relevant. Different syn-seeds have been assessed in highly characterized research cohorts, but data assessing type and frequency in patients from routine clinical encounters are lacking. Hence, our objective was to determine frequency, type, and clinical association of different syn-seeds in CSF in a large cohort from a movement disorders (MDs) clinic. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included consecutive patients from a MD clinic between 2009 and 2025. CSF was tested with synSAA and clinical data derived from medical records. RESULTS: We recruited 1,059 patients (mean age 70.5 ± 10.5 years; 38.4% female; mean disease duration 4.0 ± 4.6 years). Syn-seeds were detected in 54.2% of patients, with type1-seeds predominating (88.5%). High synSAA positivity was observed in Parkinson disease (PD) (84.7%), dementia with LB (93.4%), MSA (84.5%), isolated REM-sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) (80.0%), and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) with PD (87.0%). Undetermined hypokinetic MD showed 53.7% positivity. Moderate proportions (∼25-33%) were detected in Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal syndrome, and idiopathic NPH without PD, while other neurologic disorders showed 20.9% positivity. Type2-seeds were the major seed type in MSA (79.6% of syn-seeds) and minor type in PD (6.2%), PSP (9.1%), and undetermined hypokinetic MD (13.8%). Overall, type2-seeds were present in only 2.6% of non-MSA patients. Patients with type1-seeds had worse olfaction and more hallucinations. Multivariable regression identified impaired olfaction (OR = 0.67 per point increase of identified smells out of 12, higher scores indicating better olfaction) significantly associated with type1-seeds. DISCUSSION: Our results provide reference data on syn-seed frequency in routine clinical patients, demonstrating that type1-seeds indicate common underlying syn-pathology or copathology associated with hyposmia and hallucinations. Type2-seeds are specific to MSA and detection of type2-seeds outside the clinical MSA spectrum can improve diagnosis of patients with atypical presentations because our results match neuropathologic MSA studies. In vivo identification of different seed types will improve diagnosis, clinical trial stratification, and development of targeted therapies.

global_hot_topics.title: Label-free multi-metric pipeline for reproducible clustering of single-cell RNA-seq cell types.
global_hot_topics.authors: Zachary Yousef; Jonah Simone; Dylan Klein; Avinav Bhuyan; Heejoo Jen Cho; Priya Bhatt; Jiawei Wu; Hongyi Wang
global_hot_topics.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed our ability to identify cell types and explore cellular diversity. However, determining whether apparent cell subtypes represent true biological populations or artifacts of data analysis remains a major challenge. To address this issue, we developed scClustBench, an open-source benchmarking framework that evaluates cluster quality, stability, and reproducibility across multiple analytical approaches. Rather than relying on a single clustering method, scClustBench tests whether proposed cell subtypes can be consistently recovered. We applied scClustBench to a mouse retinal dataset containing bipolar cells, which are known to exhibit subtype diversity, and rod photoreceptors, for which subtype classification remains controversial. The framework consistently identified reproducible bipolar cell subtypes across analytical methods. In contrast, while some rod photoreceptor clusters appeared stable during resampling analyses, they could not be reproduced across embedding methods, suggesting that these partitions do not represent robust biological subtypes. Additional analyses using simulated and external datasets demonstrated that scClustBench reliably distinguishes meaningful cellular heterogeneity from analytical artifacts. These findings provide a practical framework for rigorous interpretation of single-cell transcriptomic data.

global_hot_topics.title: Protein spherical nucleic acids enable multivalent display of TLR9 agonists for enhanced cancer immunotherapy.
global_hot_topics.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
global_hot_topics.authors: Taokun Luo; Zhenyu Han; Young Jun Kim; Vinzenz Mayer; Alex Cushing; Chad A Mirkin
global_hot_topics.abstract: Precise control over nanoparticle composition and molecular architecture remains a fundamental challenge in nanomedicine, limiting systematic exploration of therapeutic design and biological function. Here, we report structurally defined protein spherical nucleic acids (ProSNAs) comprising ferritin nanocages densely functionalized with Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) agonist, immunostimulatory oligonucleotide shell for cancer immunotherapy. ProSNAs are rapidly internalized by immune cells, elicit potent innate immune activation, and exhibit prolonged intratumoral retention with preferential uptake by myeloid cells. These responses promote dendritic cell maturation, polarize macrophages toward an antitumor phenotype, and stimulate robust CD8+ T cell-mediated immunity. Across murine melanoma, colon adenocarcinoma, and triple-negative breast cancer models, a single intratumoral administration of ProSNAs induces durable tumor regression, suppresses metastatic progression, and synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade. Taken together, these findings establish ProSNAs as a structurally defined, myeloid-targeting nanomedicine platform for programmable cancer immunotherapy.

global_hot_topics.title: Tumor cell-intrinsic E47 functions as a critical suppressor in antitumor immunity via the FBXL2-PD-L1 axis.
global_hot_topics.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
global_hot_topics.authors: Rongtian Guo; Kun Wang; Jing Xu; Xin Lian; Ruixiao Bai; Xiaoli Chen; Haorui Zheng; Jiexin Gao
global_hot_topics.abstract: The transcription factor E47, encoded by the TCF3 gene, is essential for B and T cell lineage commitment and development. However, whether tumor cell-intrinsic E47 contributes to tumor immunosurveillance remains unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that E47 functions as a critical suppressor of antitumor immunity. Clinical analyses reveal that increased intratumoral TCF3 expression is associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Silencing of E47 in tumor cells markedly inhibits tumor growth, increases infiltration of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, and decreases PD-L1 expression. Mechanistically, E47 transcriptionally represses FBXL2, which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes PD-L1 polyubiquitination at K270 and proteasomal degradation. Restoration of FBXL2 effectively reverses E47-induced PD-L1 upregulation and tumor growth. Strikingly, Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug nebivolol, an activator of FBXL2, significantly enhances antitumor immunity and improves the efficacy of CTLA-4 blockade therapy in syngeneic tumor mouse models. Together, this study uncovers the E47-FBXL2 axis as a critical pathway governing PD-L1 stability and antitumor immunity, highlighting its therapeutic potential for improving the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.

global_hot_topics.journal: Journal of cell communication and signaling
global_hot_topics.authors: Hai-Qi Liang; Sheng-Hua Deng; Yu-Qi Liang; Qiu-Ju Wei; Bin-Tong Yin; Yao-Yu Wang; Ren-Jun Nong; Chao-Bin Li
global_hot_topics.abstract: The prevalence of hyperuricemia (HUA) is continuously increasing and HUA may eventually develop into irreversible hyperuricemic nephropathy (HN). Injured proximal tubule (PT) in the HUA microenvironment plays an important role in the progression of HN. However, the underlying pathological mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between HUA kidneys and control groups were screened from bulk RNA sequencing data to identify abnormally activated signaling. Subsequently, PT cell-subtypes related to injury and repair were identified in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Cellular functions of injured PT cells were identified via pseudotime analysis, cell communication analysis, and in silico perturbation. Additionally, spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics analyses were combined to validate the expression correlation of signature genes and the functional changes of PT in HUA kidneys. TGF-β signaling-associated genes were upregulated in HUA kidneys. Injured and repairing PT cell subtypes were identified in HUA kidneys with an increased proportion of the Injured subtype and a decreased proportion of the repairing subtype. Spp1 was identified as a signature gene of PT cells and injured PT cells in HUA kidneys. As the receptor of SPP1, CD44 was specifically upregulated in injured PT. Tgfb1 and Tgfbr1 were more highly expressed in the Injured PT subtypes and exhibited spatial overlap with Spp1 and Cd44. In silico perturbation of Cd44 in the Injured cell-subcluster predicted reduced expression of TGF-β signaling-related genes. Cell communication analysis predicted potential associations between CD44+ PT cells and increased SPP1-CD44 axis signaling via autocrine/paracrine SPP1. These predicted interactions may also be linked to TGF-β-associated signaling and to potential pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic functional programs in fibroblasts, macrophages, and dendritic cells (DCs). Additionally, spatial proteomics supported the high expression of TGF-β signaling-related proteins in PT. Computational analyses suggest that CD44+ PT cells are associated with TGF-β-related signaling and may interact with fibroblasts and immune cells through the SPP1-CD44 axis, representing the candidate cell population in the progression of inflammation and fibrosis in HN.

medical_news.title: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain
medical_news.abstract: Blockbuster weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro may do more than help people shed pounds, with growing evidence suggesting they could also influence brain health. Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.

medical_news.title: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half
medical_news.abstract: A powerful experimental weight-loss drug helped people with knee osteoarthritis lose about 25% of their body weight at the highest dose, while roughly two-thirds experienced at least a 50% reduction in knee pain. The findings suggest retatrutide could transform treatment for millions suffering from painful arthritis, although its ability to prevent further joint damage remains unknown.

medical_news.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
medical_news.abstract: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
